outcome: The Lenstra-Pomerance-Wagstaff conjecture (infinitely many Mersenne primes, equivalently infinitely many even perfect numbers) remains completely open. Since 26 January 2024 the only concrete developments are: (1) discovery of the 52nd known Mersenne prime, 2^136279841-1, on 12 October 2024 by Luke Durant via GIMPS using a GPU-based cloud infrastructure; (2) GIMPS completing exhaustive trial-checking of all exponents below 136,279,841 as of 18 June 2025, a search-completeness milestone; and (3) a stream of unvetted preprints (2024-2025) claiming a proof, none of which have been accepted, digested by experts, or survived scrutiny. None of these change the status of the conjecture itself.

disputes.summary: Multiple independent, uncoordinated preprint claims to have proved the conjecture have appeared since 2024 (e.g. a June 2024 ResearchGate paper 'Proof of the existence of infinite number of Mersenne primes' using a 'complementary prime sieve' / 'Dénes type Symmetric Prime Number theorem'; a June 2024 ResearchGate paper 'Proof of Mersenne Conjecture' via a Pigeonhole Principle argument; and an October 2025 preprints.org manuscript 'There Are Infinitely Many Mersenne Primes' by an independent researcher, Michael Mark Anthony, explicitly marked 'not peer-reviewed'). None have been accepted by a journal, digested by an expert, or received any public rebuttal/endorsement from a working number theorist; they appear to be part of the long-standing pattern of amateur claimed proofs of famous open conjectures that periodically surface on preprint servers.

summary: No change to the conjecture's open status has occurred since 26 January 2024. The conjecture (infinitely many Mersenne primes / infinitely many even perfect numbers) is an infinitude question, which under §3.1 only moves when it is actually answered — narrowing the search space or finding one more example does not count. Two genuine, verifiable developments occurred in the window: GIMPS/Luke Durant found the 52nd known Mersenne prime, 2^136279841-1 (41,024,320 digits), on 12 October 2024, using a distributed GPU cloud infrastructure across 17 countries; this is a new largest example, not progress on the infinitude question, and per §3.1 does not change the bullet. Separately, GIMPS completed exhaustive double-checking of all exponents below 136,279,841 by 18 June 2025 — again a search-completeness milestone, not a change to whether infinitely many exist. On the AI side, the Durant discovery is explicitly NOT an AI story: press coverage states Durant's stated motivation was to demonstrate that GPUs (typically associated with AI/ML workloads) are useful 'for more than AI' — i.e. the GPUs ran the deterministic Lucas-Lehmer primality test, not any learned model, so ai_role is 'none'. I also found and traced an unrelated news item (a ChatGPT-assisted resolution of a 60-year-old Erdős primitive-set conjecture) that a search briefly surfaced under similar phrasing; I confirmed by reading the source that it has nothing to do with Mersenne primes and excluded it. On the claimed-proof side, I found at least four independent unvetted claims of a proof posted to ResearchGate and Preprints.org between 2024 and 2025 (one flagged by triage, three found independently by me), none peer-reviewed, none digested, and none discussed by any credible source as correct — consistent with the long history of amateur 'proofs' of this exact conjecture (a genuinely retracted professional attempt by Janusz Czelakowski via Studia Logica exists in the literature, but that retraction was in October 2022, well before the frozen revision, so it is out of window and not part of this record's finding). No arXiv preprint, Terence Tao blog post, Quanta piece, or other expert-authored source discusses any progress on the actual infinitude question in the 26 Jan 2024–present window. I am satisfied this is a well-evidenced 'nothing happened' record.
competing_reading: None of the found preprints plausibly changes the classification, since none carry any indicium of correctness (no journal acceptance, no expert endorsement, no citation by credible sources) — but if any of the 2024-2025 preprint claims were later validated by an expert without my finding evidence of that, the record would need to move from 'open' to 'claimed' or better. I judge this unlikely given the total absence of any expert commentary treating these claims seriously.
what_would_settle_it: A citation of any of the preprint proofs by a credible number theorist (positive or as a debunking), or a retraction/correction notice on preprints.org or ResearchGate for the 2024-2025 claims, would confirm they remain dead ends; conversely, any digestion (blog post, MathOverflow thread, journal submission record) treating one as a serious candidate would change the status.
